title: Alaska Airlines Flight 261 Flew on One Jackscrew. The Airline Extended the Lubrication Interval.
title_candidates: Alaska Airlines Flight 261 Flew on One Jackscrew. The Airline Extended the Lubrication Interval.
Alaska Airlines Flight 261 Turned on One Jackscrew Nut. Ninety Per Cent of Its Threads Were Gone.
Alaska Airlines Flight 261 Was Measured Once. There Is No Record of What the Number Said.
description:
There is a gauge in this story. It is about the size of a pocket watch, it costs less than a good pair of boots, and it has one needle.

For eleven minutes on a January afternoon in 2000, two pilots fought an aeroplane that would not let them climb, level, or slow down. The thing that failed had been measured. Once. Two and a half years earlier. So why is there no record of what that measurement said?

On a McDonnell Douglas MD-80, the whole horizontal surface at the back is moved by a single steel screw standing vertically inside the fin, with a nut travelling along it on two spiral threads. Thirty-two turns of steel, in total, holding the tail of an aeroplane onto the rest of it.

It is the thirty-first of January, 2000. The load sheet for Alaska Airlines flight 261, an MD-83, records ten passengers in first class, seventy in coach, and five crew. Eighty-eight people. At about ten to four in the afternoon, the autopilot disconnects. The tail has stopped moving. Not slipped. Not drifted. Stopped.

On the radio, the first officer tells a controller they have a jammed stabilizer and are maintaining altitude with difficulty. The two of them then hold the aeroplane by hand for ten more minutes. Twenty seconds after they decide to stop experimenting and fly it in, it pitches over. Nobody survives.

Probable cause: a loss of airplane pitch control resulting from the in-flight failure of the horizontal stabilizer trim system jackscrew assembly's acme nut threads. The thread failure was caused by excessive wear resulting from Alaska Airlines' insufficient lubrication of the jackscrew assembly. Then three contributing factors: two extended maintenance intervals, the FAA's approval of both, and the absence of a fail-safe mechanism. One cause. Three contributing factors. Two of which are approvals.

The threads of the nut were recovered, wrapped around the screw. About ninety per cent of the thread thickness had worn away before what was left sheared off. A jackscrew worn to the maximum the rules allow in service has about twenty-two per cent gone. This one was at ninety.

The manufacturer recommended greasing this screw every six hundred to nine hundred flight hours. In March 1985, Alaska Airlines greased it every seven hundred. In March 1987, every five hundred. In July 1988, every thousand. In February 1991, every twelve hundred. In December 1994, every sixteen hundred. And in July 1996 it came off the flight-hour schedule altogether, onto a card with a maximum interval of eight months and no flight-hour limit at all. At the time of the accident, Alaska Airlines' lubrication interval for the jackscrew assembly was more than four hundred per cent greater than it was in 1987. The investigation did not determine what information, if any, was presented as justification for those extensions.

None of this was hidden. On the twenty-ninth of May, 1984, sixteen years earlier, McDonnell Douglas issued a service letter to operators: in the lubrication passages of two returned assemblies, the grease was dry, and without evidence of recent renewal. Nor is this a story about one airline: of two hundred and fourteen assemblies later sent for overhaul, thirteen came in past the limit.

There was a second line of defence: clamp a fixture to the tail, apply a torque, and read the movement off a dial indicator. The gauge with the one needle. If the reading is between three thousandths of an inch and forty thousandths, the assembly stays on the aeroplane. Above forty, it comes off. And before July 2000, five months after this accident, a reading that came out inside the limits was not required to be recorded anywhere. A pass produced silence, and silence is indistinguishable from a good result.

The accident aeroplane's last end play check was on the twenty-seventh of September, 1997. The mechanic who performed it told investigators: I don't remember the exact number, but it was below forty thousandths, I believe. At the time of the accident, Alaska Airlines had exactly one restraining fixture in its entire inventory, at Oakland. It had been made in-house, and it did not meet the manufacturer's required specifications.

A federal grand jury looked at all of this. In December 2001, prosecutors stated that no charges would be filed. Nobody was charged. Not the airline, not a manager, not the mechanic.

Tonight, somewhere, a mechanic is clamping a fixture to the tail of an aeroplane and watching a needle settle. And whatever it says, it goes in the file. That is the whole difference.

Prime Documentary makes long-form documentaries about ordinary people and the systems that fail around them. This episode is built from the National Transportation Safety Board's aircraft accident report on this flight. No criminal outcome appears in it because there was none.

This film contains AI-assisted visualization: symbolic reconstruction, no real likenesses. Generated imagery is not evidence and is not presented as an authentic record.
